planting.note: Sow cold-stratified seed or set out container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist loam in full sun; Japanese larch grows fastest of the larches and tolerates heavier, wetter soils than European larch.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, giving this fast-growing pyramidal conifer room to reach 40-70 feet with a broad, somewhat pendulous branching habit. Needles emerge soft blue-green in spring on short spur shoots, deepening through summer before turning a striking orange-gold in autumn and dropping, revealing attractive reddish winter bark and small rounded cones with reflexed scale tips that distinguish it from European larch. Widely planted in forestry plantations and as a fast-screening or specimen tree, it tolerates wetter and heavier soils than Larix decidua and resists larch canker better. Dwarf and weeping selections such as 'Diane' and 'Stiff Weeper' are popular for smaller gardens, though the species itself remains the standard choice for naturalistic plantings and windbreaks.

planting.note: Sow stratified seed or plant container stock in spring in full sun on well-drained, moist soil; Siberian larch is among the most cold-hardy conifers on earth and establishes readily once past the seedling stage.

directions: Site in full sun on well-drained soil, choosing this exceptionally cold-hardy conifer where winter temperatures routinely fall well below zero — few ornamental trees tolerate the extremes of the Siberian taiga as readily. The narrow, dense, pyramidal crown bears soft, light-green needles in spring that turn clear golden-yellow before dropping in autumn, and the pale, flaky bark brightens the winter landscape. Growth is somewhat slower than Japanese or European larch, and the species is notably more drought- and heat-sensitive, performing best in cold, continental climates with reliable soil moisture rather than in mild or humid regions. Valued in northern shelterbelts, arboreta, and cold-climate specimen plantings where more common larches struggle.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed; jimsonweed germinates best in warm soil and resents transplanting due to its sensitive taproot.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow for their coarse, sprawling habit. This rank-smelling, bushy annual bears large, trumpet-shaped white to pale violet flowers that open in late afternoon and through the night, followed by the distinctive large, egg-shaped, densely spiny seed capsules that give the plant its 'thorn apple' nickname. Every part of the plant is highly toxic if ingested, so site it away from children, pets, and livestock and handle with gloves when weeding or removing spent plants. Widely naturalized across North America as a disturbed-ground colonizer, it self-seeds readily and is best grown as a curiosity specimen or in a contained bed rather than mixed borders.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container-grown nursery trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Victorian box transplants best as a young, actively growing specimen and establishes quickly in mild climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving this dense, glossy-leaved tree room to form a broad, rounded canopy over time. In spring it produces small, waxy, cream-colored flowers in dense clusters whose orange-blossom fragrance can perfume an entire garden from a considerable distance, followed by orange seed capsules that split to reveal sticky orange-coated seeds beloved by birds. Native to eastern Australia, it is widely planted as a street and screening tree in Mediterranean and subtropical climates but has become an aggressive naturalized weed in parts of California, Hawaii, Jamaica, and South Africa, so gardeners in those regions should deadhead promptly or choose a non-invasive alternative. Tolerates clay soils, salt spray, and light shade better than many broadleaf evergreens.

planting.note: Propagate by semi-ripe cuttings in summer or plant container stock in spring in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; wild jasmine is the hardiest of the shrubby jasmines and establishes readily once rooted.

directions: Plant in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, where this bushy, semi-evergreen to deciduous Mediterranean native forms an upright thicket of slender, angled green stems clothed in small, glossy, trifoliate leaves. Clusters of small, unscented, bright yellow flowers appear from late spring into summer, followed by black, pea-sized berries that ripen in autumn and persist into winter. Unlike the twining vine-type jasmines grown for fragrance, this free-standing shrub is valued for drought tolerance, limestone-soil adaptability, and informal hedging or bank cover in dry gardens. Prune after flowering to maintain a compact shape, as old wood can become leggy and sparse.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown or scarified-seed-grown stock in spring in full sun to part shade on well-drained soil; Chinese sumac suckers freely once established and spreads to form thickets.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, allowing room for this large, suckering shrub or small tree to spread, as it readily forms colonies from root sprouts. Large pinnately compound leaves turn vivid orange-red in autumn, and showy, upright panicles of small greenish-white flowers in late summer give way to flattened, orange-red, hairy drupes that persist into winter and attract birds. The tree is best known as the host of the gall-forming aphid Melaphis chinensis, whose galls ('Chinese galls' or 'wu bei zi') are harvested and dried for use as a tannin-rich astringent in traditional medicine and natural dyeing. Give it room away from refined beds since root suckers must be controlled annually to prevent thicket formation.
